I am a 74-year-old woman who has farmed the same plot of land in Quzhou County since I was a young bride. I never went to school, but I know this land better than anyone. Every year I grow the same crops my family has grown for generations — winter wheat followed by summer maize. That is what the North China Plain is made for. I have about 4 mu of land, which is all I can manage now at my age.

This autumn, I will sow wheat again. I will buy Jimai 22 seeds from the seed shop in town — it is an improved variety that does well here, and the neighbors all say it is reliable. I will rotary-till the land before sowing, because the soil gets hard over summer and the wheat needs a soft bed. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer as basal dressing — about 100 jin per mu — and then topdress with urea in spring when the wheat starts to green up. I know the wheat needs nitrogen to grow strong. I will irrigate three or four times: once before winter to help it survive the cold, and two or three times in spring when the weather turns dry. I will spray herbicide once after sowing to keep the weeds down, and maybe insecticide once or twice if I see pests. I expect to harvest about 1000 jin per mu around early June.

As soon as the wheat comes off, I will sow maize straight away — no need to till again, just plant directly into the stubble. I will use Denghai 605, a hybrid seed that gives good yield. The maize needs less irrigation than wheat, maybe twice over the summer. I will fertilize it with compound fertilizer at planting and add urea when it is knee-high. I will watch for corn borers and spray insecticide if they appear, and put down herbicide once. By October, I should get about 1100 jin per mu of maize.

This is the rotation I trust. It feeds me and leaves some grain to sell. At my age, I do not want to experiment with new crops — I want to grow what I know will keep me fed.
